article.headline: Goldman's Photonics Map Left Out the Terrain That Matters
article.lede: Goldman Sachs sees a $154 billion optical-networking market by 2028, but its supply-chain map skips the foundries, wafer growers, and equipment makers that actually make chips move light. A retail investor's annotated rebuttal names names.
article.body:
Goldman Sachs projects that the market for optical networking hardware will expand roughly ninefold — from about $15 billion today to $154 billion by the time NVIDIA's Rubin Ultra platform is in full production — with **co-packaged optics** (CPO, a design that fuses laser transceivers directly onto a switch chip to slash power and latency) accounting for $91 billion of that figure. The bank's report, circulated in early 2025, has become the photonics sector's equivalent of a treasure map. The post argues, with some justification, that Goldman has drawn the coastline but left the interior blank.

The most pointed omission concerns substrates. Every silicon photonics chip manufactured at TSMC begins life as a *photonics-grade silicon-on-insulator* (Photonics-SOI) wafer — a sandwich of ultra-thin silicon atop a buried oxide layer, engineered to guide light with minimal loss. **Soitec** (ticker: SOI, Paris) is the only supplier approved by TSMC, Tower Semiconductor, and GlobalFoundries for volume Photonics-SOI production. Two decades of process know-how and tight qualification cycles make that position nearly impossible to replicate quickly. Yet the Goldman deck apparently treats the wafer as a commodity input.

The *epitaxial layer* — the crystalline film grown atop a base wafer to produce active optical structures like lasers and detectors — represents a second invisible link. **IQE plc** (LON: IQE) grows these compound semiconductor films; it recently launched a 6-inch foundry platform for silicon photonics customers and secured multiple Tier 1 design wins for AI data-centre laser and detector products. The post cites its £400 million market capitalisation against Sumitomo Electric's roughly $52 billion and calls the gap an anomaly. That framing has some merit — IQE's role in the laser supply chain is structurally indispensable — though small-cap liquidity risk and execution uncertainty argue for caution before labelling any multiple "absurd." The market cap figure cited in the tweet ($400M) is somewhat dated; as of May 2026, IQE trades closer to a £545 million capitalisation, so the specific asymmetry claim needs updating even if the directional logic holds.

On equipment, **Aixtron** (XETRA: AIXA) manufactures *MOCVD reactors* — metal-organic chemical vapour deposition systems that bake compound semiconductors into precise crystalline layers at extreme temperatures. Every major laser maker (Sumitomo, Lumentum, VPEC) uses them. Aixtron's first-quarter 2026 order intake rose 30% year-over-year to €171 million, with optoelectronics comprising nearly 70% of new orders; the company subsequently raised its full-year revenue guidance to €560 million. **Aehr Test Systems** (NASDAQ: AEHR) provides wafer-level burn-in — stress-testing photonic chips while still on the wafer, before dicing, which is both cheaper and more reliable than package-level testing. Aehr booked $37 million in a single quarter early in 2026 and won a new silicon photonics transceiver customer in March. **LPKF Laser** (XETRA: LPKF) adds a third equipment angle: its proprietary *LIDE* process (Laser-Induced Deep Etching) creates precision through-holes in glass panels, enabling glass-based substrates that can also guide light — a natural fit for CPO modules where both electrical and optical interconnects must coexist at microscopic scales.

**Tower Semiconductor** (NASDAQ: TSEM), the independent foundry the post calls arguably the leading photonics fabricator, generated $228 million in silicon photonics revenue in 2025 — more than double the prior year — and is committing $920 million in capital expenditure to expand capacity, with over 70% of that capacity already reserved by customers through 2028. That level of demand commitment is unusual in the foundry business and lends credibility to the supercycle thesis. **Sivers Semiconductors** (Nasdaq Stockholm: SIVE), the Swedish maker of *indium phosphide* (InP) lasers, recently demonstrated wafer-scale hybrid integration of its DFB lasers onto a 300mm silicon photonics wafer with sub-500nm alignment — a milestone that matters because the shortage of light sources is the most widely cited bottleneck in CPO commercialisation. Sivers posted record revenues of SEK 304 million in 2025, up 25%, though its opportunity pipeline ($453 million) still dwarfs its current run-rate, suggesting the ramp is front-loaded with engineering wins rather than production revenue.

The broader critique — that sell-side ecosystem maps systematically underweight the picks-and-shovels layer — is well-trodden but not wrong. Goldman's forecast numbers are genuine; the supply chain analysis is, by the author's account, incomplete. Whether the named small-caps can convert structural necessity into durable pricing power is a different question, and one the tweet elides. Capital cycles have a way of attracting competition to exactly the nodes that look most indispensable.

concepts.definition: A chip architecture that integrates optical transceivers directly onto the same package as a switch or compute chip, replacing electrical signalling between them with light. CPO dramatically reduces power consumption and latency compared to pluggable optical modules that sit at the edge of a rack. Goldman Sachs projects CPO will represent $91 billion of the $154 billion optical-networking market by 2028.

A wafer architecture in which a thin layer of silicon sits atop an electrically insulating buried oxide. In photonics, the refractive-index contrast between the silicon and the oxide confines light in waveguides, enabling chips that route optical signals much as conventional chips route electrons. Photonics-grade SOI requires tighter uniformity specs than standard SOI used in logic chips.

A crystalline film deposited atom-by-atom atop a base substrate, matching its crystal structure. In compound semiconductors like indium phosphide (InP) or gallium arsenide (GaAs), the epitaxial layer defines the active region of a laser or detector. Growing it reproducibly at commercial volumes requires MOCVD equipment and significant process know-how.

A reactor-based manufacturing process in which metallic precursor gases are flowed over a heated wafer, depositing precise atomic layers of compound semiconductor material. MOCVD is the primary growth technique for III-V semiconductor lasers and detectors used in optical communications. Aixtron and Veeco are the two dominant equipment suppliers.

A reliability screening process that applies elevated temperature and voltage or current to semiconductor chips while they are still part of an intact wafer, before they are cut into individual dies. Testing at the wafer stage is cheaper than package-level testing because defective chips are identified before the cost of packaging is incurred. Photonic chips require specialised burn-in because light output degrades through different failure modes than purely electronic devices.

A compound semiconductor composed of indium and phosphorus, notable for its direct bandgap and high electron mobility. InP is the substrate of choice for lasers and photodetectors operating in the 1.3–1.6 µm wavelength range used in telecommunications and data-centre optics. Supply of InP substrates is geographically concentrated, making it a cited geopolitical risk in the photonics supply chain.

LPKF's proprietary process for creating precise micro-holes and channels in glass substrates using an ultrashort-pulse laser followed by a wet etch step. The technique enables glass-core substrates for advanced semiconductor packaging, offering advantages over silicon interposers in electrical loss and optical transparency — properties increasingly relevant for packages that must carry both electrical and optical signals simultaneously.

article.fact_check: The tweet states IQE has a '$400M mcap' versus Sumitomo's '$52B mcap'. The IQE figure appears to reference an earlier trading period; as of May 2026, IQE's market capitalisation is approximately £545 million (~$680 million at current rates), making the stated asymmetry numerically outdated even if qualitatively valid. The claim that Tower Semiconductor is 'tripling its capacity' is broadly consistent with public disclosures: Tower has committed $920 million in capex and targets silicon photonics wafer starts more than five times Q4 2025 monthly shipments by end-2026, which exceeds a simple tripling. Goldman's forecast of $154 billion total value TAM by the Rubin Ultra cycle (mainly 2028) with CPO at $91 billion is confirmed by the OCR text extracted from the report image. The claim that AIXTRON reactors are used by 'EVERY listed laser manufacturer' is a reasonable characterisation given Aixtron's 70-90% MOCVD market share in relevant product segments, though not independently verifiable to the letter.

ticker_sive.name: Sivers Semiconductors AB (publ)
ticker_sive.blurb: Sivers designs and manufactures indium phosphide (InP) distributed feedback lasers and optical amplifiers used inside high-speed optical transceivers, automotive LiDAR systems and satellite communications terminals. Its photonics business is one of the few independent western sources of the laser dies that go into AI-data-centre optical links, alongside larger incumbents such as Coherent and Lumentum. A separate wireless unit supplies 5G millimetre-wave RF chips. The company has been preparing a spin-off and potential dual Nasdaq New York listing of its photonics subsidiary.
ticker_sive.recent: Shares ran from roughly SEK 4 at the start of 2026 to a close of SEK 55.95 in early May, a year-to-date gain of about 1,247%, on customer wins including a 1.6T linear-drive optical module collaboration with Jabil announced 15 April 2026 and a LiDAR ramp scheduled for Q4 2026 with up to $138m of cumulative lifetime revenue. 2025 net sales were SEK 304m (+25% YoY) but the after-tax loss was SEK 186m, prompting an April 2026 directed issue of 8.62m shares at SEK 14.50 raising about SEK 125m at roughly 2.5% dilution. Photonics experts and Swedish business media have publicly questioned whether the rally has run ahead of fundamentals.

ticker_iqe.name: IQE plc
ticker_iqe.exchange: London Stock Exchange (LON: IQE); OTC: IQEPF
ticker_iqe.blurb: IQE plc is the world's leading independent manufacturer of compound semiconductor epitaxial wafers, supplying the active crystalline layers that underpin lasers, detectors, and RF devices. The company operates through three segments — Wireless, Photonics, and CMOS++ — with its Photonics segment providing InP and GaAs epi-wafers used in optical transceivers for data centres, LiDAR, and 3D sensing. Headquartered in Cardiff, Wales, IQE's commercial position rests on process know-how that takes years to replicate and tight qualification relationships with Tier 1 customers.
ticker_iqe.recent: In 2025, IQE reported full-year revenue of approximately £97 million, entering 2026 with a strong first-quarter order book. The company secured multiple Tier 1 design wins for AI and hyperscale data-centre laser and detector products and launched a 6-inch foundry platform for silicon photonics customers. As of May 2026, IQE trades at approximately 41p on the London Stock Exchange, giving it a market capitalisation of roughly £545 million.

ticker_lpkf.name: LPKF Laser & Electronics SE
ticker_lpkf.blurb: LPKF Laser & Electronics is a German manufacturer of laser systems for electronics production, best known in the semiconductor packaging world for its proprietary LIDE (Laser-Induced Deep Etching) process. LIDE uses an ultrashort-pulse laser followed by a selective wet etch to create precise through-glass vias (TGVs) and complex 3D structures in glass panels without cracking or thermal damage. Glass substrates processed with LIDE can carry both electrical interconnects and optical waveguides in the same package — a property directly relevant to co-packaged optics (CPO) architectures. The company is headquartered in Garbsen, Germany and listed on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange.
ticker_lpkf.recent: LPKF reported a slight improvement in full-year 2025 earnings while announcing a broader group realignment as it pivots its commercial focus toward advanced semiconductor packaging, particularly glass substrates for AI infrastructure. In April 2025, the company announced a collaboration with Onto Innovation aimed at accelerating mass production of glass core substrates. As of early 2026, the LIDE process has moved from customer demonstrations into initial production qualifications at several advanced packaging customers, though volume revenue from glass substrates remained limited and management guided that a full commercial ramp would extend into 2027.

ticker_soi.name: Soitec SA
ticker_soi.blurb: Soitec is a Grenoble-based manufacturer of engineered semiconductor wafers — most notably silicon-on-insulator (SOI) substrates produced via its proprietary Smart Cut process. It supplies wafers, not chips, and dominates niche segments: roughly 70%+ share of RF-SOI used in 5G smartphone radios, and an estimated 95%+ share of photonics-grade SOI, the substrate beneath nearly every silicon photonic integrated circuit. Its product lines include RF-SOI, FD-SOI for low-power logic, POI for RF filters, and photonics-SOI for optical interconnect chips. Mobile communications still account for the majority of revenue (about 546 million EUR of FY2025's 891 million EUR), but the photonics line has become the market's focal point.
ticker_soi.recent: Shares bottomed at 41.77 EUR on March 9, 2026 after a multi-year derating tied to smartphone wafer oversupply, then rallied violently as investors re-rated the photonics franchise around NVIDIA's co-packaged optics (CPO) roadmap. By April 17 Bloomberg called Soitec Europe's best-performing stock of 2026; analysts at Citigroup, Oddo BHF and Deutsche Bank lifted price targets in April. On May 4, 2026 the stock printed 153.55 EUR, up 517.41% YTD with a market capitalization of 5.29 billion EUR. Full-year results are scheduled for May 27, 2026; valuation has stretched to a P/E around 394 against a sector average near 29, with revenue still down roughly 10% year-over-year.

ticker_tsem.name: Tower Semiconductor
ticker_tsem.blurb: Tower Semiconductor is an Israeli specialty foundry that fabricates analogue, mixed-signal, and photonic chips across 200mm and 300mm wafer lines. Unlike pure-play logic foundries such as TSMC, Tower focuses on differentiated process technologies where customers need more than commodity nodes — silicon photonics, silicon-germanium (SiGe), radio-frequency CMOS, and power management. Tower's silicon photonics platform (SiPho) is widely regarded as one of the most mature independent photonics foundry offerings, supporting both passive waveguide structures and active electro-optic components on the same wafer. The company operates fabs in Israel, the United States, Japan, and Italy.
ticker_tsem.recent: Tower committed $920 million in capital expenditure to silicon photonics and SiGe capacity — a 40% increase from a plan announced just three months earlier — with over 70% of that reserved or prepaid by customers through 2028. In November 2025, the company launched a dedicated CPO Foundry offering with 300mm wafer-bonding technology and targeted more than quintupling its monthly SiPho wafer shipments between Q4 2025 and late 2026. In March 2026, Tower announced full ownership of its 300mm Fab 7 facility in Japan to support this expansion, positioning itself to challenge GlobalFoundries for the top-ranked independent silicon photonics foundry slot.

ticker_aixa.name: Aixtron SE
ticker_aixa.blurb: Aixtron SE is the dominant supplier of metal-organic chemical vapour deposition (MOCVD) reactors — the industrial ovens that grow compound semiconductor films atom-by-atom onto wafers. With a 70–90% market share across most of its product portfolio, Aixtron equipment is found in the fabs of virtually every laser diode manufacturer. The company is based in Herzogenrath, Germany, and its technology is material-agnostic across arsenides, phosphides, nitrides, and carbides, spanning markets from telecoms lasers to power electronics.
ticker_aixa.recent: Aixtron's Q1 2026 revenue fell 47% year-over-year to €59 million due to seasonal delivery timing, but order intake surged 30% to €171 million with optoelectronics comprising nearly 70% of new orders. The company subsequently raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to €560 million (±€30 million) with an EBIT margin of 17–20%, up from prior guidance of €520 million. Its G10-AsP platform, designed for arsenide/phosphide lasers used in AI data-centre transceivers, was the primary volume driver.

ticker_aehr.name: Aehr Test Systems
ticker_aehr.blurb: Aehr Test Systems designs and manufactures wafer-level burn-in and test equipment for semiconductors, with a specialisation in silicon carbide (SiC) power devices, gallium nitride (GaN), and — increasingly — silicon photonics chips. Its flagship FOX-XP system stress-tests devices while still on the wafer, before costly packaging, identifying failures at the cheapest possible point in manufacturing. Aehr claims to be the first company to ship a multi-wafer burn-in solution for silicon photonics transceivers. The company is headquartered in Fremont, California.
ticker_aehr.recent: In March 2026, Aehr won a new silicon photonics customer for its high-power FOX-XP wafer-level burn-in system targeting hyperscale data-centre optical interconnects. Quarterly bookings reached $37.2 million in the quarter ending February 2026 — a book-to-bill ratio exceeding 3.5x — with the company guiding full-year FY2026 revenue toward the high end of its $45–$50 million range. Revenue in the same quarter was $10.3 million, down from $18.3 million a year earlier, reflecting a timing gap between order intake and shipment schedules weighted toward the second half of 2026.

ticker_glw.name: Corning Incorporated
ticker_glw.blurb: Corning Incorporated is an American specialty glass and ceramics manufacturer with roots stretching back to 1851. Its Optical Communications segment — the world's largest maker of optical fibre and fibre-optic cable — has become the principal earnings engine as AI-driven data-centre construction accelerates demand for high-capacity fibre infrastructure. Corning also supplies specialty glass for displays, life sciences, and advanced semiconductor substrates, and has a developing presence in co-packaged optics component supply through collaborations with Broadcom and others. The company is headquartered in Corning, New York.
ticker_glw.recent: Corning's Optical Communications segment posted full-year 2025 sales of $6.3 billion, up 35% year-over-year, with enterprise data-centre revenue growing 61%. In early 2026, Corning signed a multiyear agreement worth up to $6 billion to supply Meta's global AI data-centre buildout with optical fibre and cable. Bank of America subsequently pegged the total scale-out revenue opportunity at $10.3 billion by 2030. Corning's internal Springboard plan now targets $6.5 billion in incremental annualised sales by end-2026.
